rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Although the original uses past tense, Asad renders the exchange in present tense to show the metaphorical question and answer continually recurring.
rows.anchor: this passage is in the past tense ("He brought forth", "He asked them", etc.), thus stressing the continuous recurrence

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Every sane person has inborn awareness of the Supreme Power through fitrah; self-indulgence or harmful surroundings may later obscure this instinctive cognition.
rows.anchor: the ability to perceive the existence of the Supreme Power is inborn in human nature (fitrah)

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: God's speaking and humanity's answer are metonyms for God's creative act and each person's existential response to it.
rows.anchor: God's "speaking" and man's "answering" is a metonym for the creative act of God and of man's existential response to it

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Asad directs readers to Appendix III for further discussion of the invisible beings.
rows.anchor: See Appendix 111.

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: People are more astray than cattle because animals follow instinct and natural needs without awareness of moral choice.
rows.anchor: inasmuch as animals follow only their instincts and natural needs and are not conscious of the possibility or necessity of a moral choice

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The verse follows the heedless ones of 7:179: they fail to discern as intended and ignore God, who embodies all perfection and is Ultimate Reality.
rows.anchor: This passage connects with the mention, at the end of the preceding verse, of "the heedless ones" who do not use their faculty of discernment

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Asma al-husna means God's attributes of perfection: ism denotes substance or intrinsic attributes, al-husna is the plural of al-ahsan, and the term is reserved for God.
rows.anchor: the term ism is, primarily, a word applied to denote the substance or the intrinsic attributes of an object under consideration

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi explains distortion of God's names as applying them to other beings or defining God through anthropomorphic relations such as father or son.
rows.anchor: by applying them to other beings or objects or, alternatively, by trying to "define" God in anthropomorphic terms and relationships, like "father" or "son" (Razi)

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The promise of requital includes the righteous of every era and community who receive God's messages and live by conviction that He is Ultimate Reality; this broadens the earlier example of Moses' people.
rows.anchor: the reference is broadened to include the righteous of all times and communities - that is, all those who are receptive to God's messages

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Asad glosses the phrase as the people not knowing from where their fate comes.
rows.anchor: without their knowing whence [it comes]

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Asad glosses kayd as a subtle scheme and directs readers to his note on 68:45.
rows.anchor: the term kayd ("subtle scheme") occurring in the next verse

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Asad glosses the changing of God's blessing as its withdrawal.
rows.anchor: I.e., withdraw.

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The statement concerns the broad law of cause and effect decreed in creation, elsewhere called sunnat Allah, and is explained in his note on 13:11.
rows.anchor: the wide implications of this statement in the context of the law of cause and effect which God has decreed on His creation

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The apostle is a human like his audience, without supernatural powers, chosen by God to convey His message.
rows.anchor: a human being like yourselves, not endowed with any supernatural powers, but only chosen by God to convey His message to you

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Da'wa is literally an invocation or call.
rows.anchor: their invocation (da'wa) therein [will be]

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Salam conveys inner peace, fulfilment, and security from every evil; Asad refers readers to his note on 5:29.
rows.anchor: the term salam and its fundamental connotation of inner peace, fulfilment, and security from all that is evil

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Asad notes that interpretations of the tannur phrase conflict and that some rely on Talmudic legends.
rows.anchor: subject to several conflicting interpretations, some of which are based on no more than Talmudic legends

rows.speaker: Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrimah
rows.claim: They interpret at-tannur as the face of the earth; Tabari, Baghawi, and Ibn Kathir transmit this as the most convincing explanation.
rows.anchor: on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrimah: "At-tannur [lit., "oven"] denotes the face of the earth."

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi says Arabs call the face of the earth tannur.
rows.anchor: Razi, too, mentions that "the Arabs call the face of the earth tannur"

rows.speaker: Qamas
rows.claim: Qamas gives tannur the meaning of any place from which water gushes.
rows.anchor: the Qamas gives as one of the meanings of tannur "any place from which water gushes forth"

rows.speaker: Ibn Kathir
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir reads fara literally as boiling over, describing torrents that turned the earth into springs, with a parallel at 54:12.
rows.anchor: The verb fara - which literally means "it boiled over" - describes the raging torrents of water which "turned the earth into springs" (Ibn Kathir

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Asad suggests the phrase points to Mediterranean inundation, expanded by torrential rain across Syria and northern Iraq, resembling flood accounts in scripture and ancient Greek, Sumerian, and Babylonian legend.
rows.anchor: seems to point to the inundation of the huge valley now covered by the Mediterranean Sea

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Zawj primarily means either member of a pair, though it can also mean a pair; the former sense best fits the phrase here.
rows.anchor: The term zawj signifies, primarily, each of the two parts of a pair, and is also used in the sense of "a pair"

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Noah was reasonably asked to bring the domesticated animals already in his possession, rather than every animal as in the Biblical narrative.
rows.anchor: it is reasonable to assume that this referred to the domesticated animals already in his possession, and not to all animals

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Those excluded from the ark were condemned because they persistently refused to acknowledge the truth; compare 11:42-43 and 11:45-47.
rows.anchor: those who stand condemned in the sight of God because of their persistent refusal to acknowledge the truth

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The diminutive ya bunayya is an affectionate address regardless of the son's age; Noah's son was grown, while Joseph addressed as such in 12:5 was a child or adolescent.
rows.anchor: The diminutive in ya bunayya (lit., "O my little son") is an expression of endearment irrespective of a son's age

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Rashid literally means not right-guided.
rows.anchor: was not right-guided (rashid)

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The Pharaoh passage in 11:96-99 connects with the earlier account of 'Ad, whose people followed every arrogant enemy of truth.
rows.anchor: connects with, and amplifies, the reference to the tribe of 'Ad, who "followed the bidding of every arrogant enemy of the truth"

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The passage addresses immoral leadership and individual responsibility: leaders and followers are equally guilty, and obedience to higher authority cannot excuse wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: the leader and the led are equally guilty, and none can be absolved of responsibility on the plea that he was but blindly following orders

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: This is an indirect allusion to relative free will, the freedom to choose right or wrong, and it concludes the surah's accounts of earlier prophets and their wrongdoing communities.
rows.anchor: This indirect allusion to man's relative free will - i.e., his freedom of choice between right and wrong - fittingly concludes the stories

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Al-ghayb means the hidden reality of the heavens and earth; Asad points to his explanation at 2:3.
rows.anchor: Lit., "God's is [the knowledge of] the hidden reality of..."

rows.speaker: Ibn 'Abbas
rows.claim: One report attributed to Ibn Abbas classifies the surah as Meccan, as cited by Suyuti.
rows.anchor: one statement attributed to Ibn 'Abbas, it is a Meccan surah (Suyuti)

rows.speaker: Ibn 'Abbas
rows.claim: Other authorities cited by Tabarani report Ibn Abbas describing the surah as Medinan.
rows.anchor: other authorities, mentioned by Tabarani, Ibn 'Abbas is reported to have described it as belonging to the Medina period

rows.speaker: Suyuti, Baghawi and Razi
rows.claim: Suyuti inclines, as do Baghawi and Razi, to a Meccan surah containing a few verses revealed in Medina.
rows.anchor: Suyuti himself inclines to the view that it

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari
rows.claim: Zamakhshari leaves the time of revelation uncertain.
rows.anchor: Zamakhshari, on the other hand, confines himself to the statement that the time of its revelation is uncertain

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The surah's title comes from the incidental mention of thunder in verse 13, which points to God's creative power manifested in nature.
rows.anchor: "thunder" occurring in verse 13

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The surah centers on God's prophetic revelation of moral truths, whose neglect brings natural consequences; Asad links this to the last paragraph of 13:31.
rows.anchor: The main theme of this surah is God's

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Those who understand moral truth and keep faith with God attain inner happiness and the best goal, consistent with the principle that God changes people's condition when they change themselves.
rows.anchor: those "who are endowed with insight... [and] are true to their bond with God"

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The idiom between a person's hands means what is evident to him, while behind him means what is beyond his ken or hidden; compare 2:255.
rows.anchor: "between his hands" denotes "something that is perceivable by him" or "evident to him", while that which is "behind him" is a metonym for something "beyond his ken"

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Mu'aqqibat is a double plural of mu'aqqib, something immediately succeeding another without interruption.
rows.anchor: a double plural of mu'aqqib, which signifies "something that comes immediately after another thing" or "succeeds another thing without interruption"

rows.speaker: Most classical commentators
rows.claim: Most classical commentators take mu'aqqibat as successive hosts of recording angels guarding each person, read before and behind as surrounding him, and render min amr Allah as by God's command.
rows.anchor: Most of the classical commentators understand by mu'aqqibat "hosts of angels", i.e., the recording angels who attend on every human being

rows.speaker: Abu Muslim al-Isfahani
rows.claim: Abu Muslim interprets mu'aqqibat as worldly powers and resources people wrongly trust to achieve aims independently of God's will; Razi quotes him.
rows.anchor: the famous commentator Abu Muslim al-Isfahani, as quoted by Razi

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Asad finds Abu Muslim's interpretation convincing and bases his translation on the worldly-protection reading rather than the angelic-guardianship reading.
rows.anchor: It is on this convincing interpretation that I have based my rendering

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The relied-on worldly guards and aids can be tangible, such as wealth or children, or intangible, such as power, status, or belief in luck; this explains the evident and hidden helpers.
rows.anchor: The worldly "guards and aids" on which a sinner relies may be tangible (like wealth, progeny, etc.) or intangible (like personal power, high social standing, or the belief in one's "luck")
